title: Career Roadmap: Ship Electrician
summary: A Ship Electrician maintains, inspects, troubleshoots and repairs electrical equipment and systems aboard ships. These systems support lighting, power distribution, motors, pumps, alarms, communication equipment and other essential shipboard operations.

facts.Current degree: Merchant Navy / Maritime Programmes (B.Sc Nautical / B.Tech Marine / GME / DNS / ETO)

about.label: Education Pathway
about.text: Merchant Navy / Maritime Programmes – Electro-Technical Officer (ETO) Course

blocks.text: A Ship Electrician maintains, inspects, troubleshoots and repairs electrical equipment and systems aboard ships. These systems support lighting, power distribution, motors, pumps, alarms, communication equipment and other essential shipboard operations.
Depending on the vessel and employer, a ship electrician may work under the supervision of an Electro-Technical Officer (ETO), Chief Engineer or another designated technical officer.
The role is important because electrical failures can affect navigation support systems, cargo operations, propulsion auxiliaries, accommodation facilities and emergency equipment.
Key responsibilities

items.text: Inspect and maintain shipboard electrical installations.
Troubleshoot faults in motors, generators, switchboards and electrical circuits.
Maintain lighting, sockets, distribution panels and electrical control systems.
Assist with preventive maintenance of pumps, fans, compressors and other electrically driven equipment.
Test electrical components using approved instruments and procedures.
Maintain records of inspections, repairs and equipment condition.
Support planned maintenance and electrical fault reporting.
Follow electrical isolation, lockout/tagout and permit-to-work procedures.
Assist authorised personnel during equipment overhauls and commissioning.
Follow shipboard safety, environmental and electrical protection requirements.

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: A Ship Electrician and an Electro-Technical Officer (ETO) are related but different roles. An ETO is an officer-level position with specific training, competency and certification requirements. A general electrician qualification does not automatically qualify someone to serve as an ETO.
The best route depends on whether you want to enter as an electrical technician or qualify for the officer-level ETO pathway.

rows.text: Develop foundations in mathematics, science and practical technical work.
Review the educational requirements of electrical and maritime programmes. Relevant ETO entry routes often require specified electrical, electronics or engineering qualifications.
Consider Electrical Engineering, Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Electronics Engineering or another qualification accepted for the intended pathway.
Learn electrical machines, power distribution, control systems, electrical safety and fault diagnosis.
Complete the approved training required for the target shipboard position.
Apply for eligible ship electrician, electrical technician or trainee ETO opportunities according to your qualifications.

blocks.text: Relevant qualifications
Potential educational routes include:

items.text: Diploma in Electrical Engineering
Diploma in Electrical and Electronics Engineering
B.E. / B.Tech in Electrical Engineering
B.E. / B.Tech in Electrical and Electronics Engineering
Relevant electronics or instrumentation qualifications, where accepted
Approved maritime Electro-Technical Officer training for eligible candidates

blocks.text: The precise qualifications accepted for ETO training depend on current maritime regulations and the approved programme.

blocks.label: Before enrolling
blocks.text: Check the current eligibility rules, approved institute status, medical fitness requirements and certification pathway with India's Directorate General of Shipping (DGS). Do not assume that a general electrical diploma or degree alone qualifies you to work as an ETO.
The following is an illustrative learning plan. Actual training duration and eligibility depend on the qualification and shipboard role you pursue.
Year 1
Foundation
Build electrical fundamentals

items.text: Study electrical circuits, voltage, current, resistance and power.
Learn AC/DC systems and basic electrical measurements.
Understand motors, transformers, generators and batteries.
Practise reading wiring diagrams and electrical symbols.
Develop safe workshop habits and technical documentation skills.

blocks.text: Year 2
Technical skills
Learn electrical maintenance

items.text: Study power distribution, switchgear, circuit protection and earthing.
Learn motor starters, relays, contactors and control circuits.
Practise using multimeters and clamp meters in supervised labs.
Understand preventive maintenance and electrical fault diagnosis.
Learn the principles of industrial automation and control systems.

blocks.text: Year 3
Application
Develop shipboard technical knowledge

items.text: Study shipboard power systems and marine electrical equipment.
Learn the functions of generators, emergency power supplies and distribution boards.
Understand alarms, sensors, control panels and automation systems.
Study electrical isolation and permit-to-work procedures.
Seek an appropriate technical internship or supervised workshop placement.

blocks.text: Final stage
Employment
Prepare for shipboard work

items.text: Complete the training required for the intended position.
Practise documenting faults, repairs and maintenance activities.
Develop knowledge of maritime safety and emergency procedures.
Verify medical fitness and seafarer documentation requirements.
Apply for eligible ship electrician, electro-technical rating or trainee ETO opportunities.

rows.text: AC/DC circuits, voltage, current, resistance and power
Switchboards, circuit breakers, fuses, earthing and protection
Fault identification, testing, diagnosis and repair documentation
Contactors, relays, starters and control circuits
Sensors, alarms, PLC fundamentals and control systems
Lighting, pumps, ventilation, emergency power and auxiliary equipment
Electrical measurement and basic sensor testing
Electrical isolation, PPE, risk assessment and permit-to-work systems
Wiring diagrams, maintenance logs and technical reports

blocks.text: Power generation and distribution
Understand how ship generators, switchboards, distribution panels and emergency power supplies support vessel operations.
Motors and auxiliary equipment
Learn the electrical principles behind pumps, fans, compressors, winches and other motor-driven machinery.
Automation and alarms
Study sensors, control panels, alarm circuits and the electrical systems used to monitor machinery conditions.
Emergency and safety systems
Understand emergency lighting, backup power, alarm systems and the importance of maintaining equipment according to approved procedures.

items.text: Digital multimeter for authorised electrical measurements.
Clamp meter for measuring current where appropriate.
Insulation resistance tester, used by trained personnel according to approved procedures.
Electrical test lamps and continuity-testing equipment.
Wiring diagrams and electrical schematics.
Motor-control and relay-training panels.
Computerised maintenance management systems (CMMS).
Technical manuals and maintenance record systems.

blocks.text: Shipboard electrical work can involve lethal voltages, stored energy and hazardous environments. Practical training must take place under appropriate supervision, using approved isolation procedures and suitable protective equipment.
Useful training areas include:

rows.text: Safe work practices, electrical hazards and isolation
Preventing equipment from being energised during maintenance
Understanding high-voltage hazards and authorised work procedures
Required safety competencies for the intended seafarer role
Responding appropriately to shipboard fire hazards
Systematic diagnosis and documentation of faults
Understanding sensors, alarms and control circuits

blocks.text: For officer-level ETO certification, follow the applicable Directorate General of Shipping and STCW requirements. India's DGS publishes the relevant maritime training guidelines and approved-course information.
DG Shipping

sections.heading: Projects to Build a Strong Portfolio

blocks.text: Complete practical projects using low-voltage training equipment or simulation environments. Do not practise on live shipboard systems without appropriate training and authorisation.

blocks.label: Project 1
blocks.text: Motor Control Circuit
Build and document a supervised training circuit using a motor-control panel, suitable protection and a control switch.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: circuit diagram, component list, operating explanation and safety checklist.

blocks.label: Project 2
blocks.text: Electrical Fault-Diagnosis Exercise
Use a simulated or instructor-approved faulty circuit to practise identifying likely faults through a structured testing process.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: fault log, test observations, diagnosis and corrective-action report.

blocks.label: Project 3
blocks.text: Shipboard Electrical Maintenance Plan
Prepare a sample preventive-maintenance schedule for lighting, motors, alarms and backup power systems.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: equipment register, maintenance intervals, inspection checklist and sample records.

blocks.text: Potential workplaces include:

items.text: Merchant shipping companies
Shipbuilding and ship-repair yards
Marine electrical contractors
Offshore support vessel operators
Marine equipment maintenance companies
Ship maintenance and repair organisations

blocks.text: Check the exact role before applying. A shore-based shipyard electrician role may have different requirements from a seagoing ship electrician position. The ETR and ETO pathways also have separate competency and training requirements.
Entry level
Electrical Trainee / Ship Electrician Trainee
Technical role
Ship Electrician / Marine Electrical Technician / Electro-Technical Rating, depending on the pathway
Officer-level pathway
Electro-Technical Officer (ETO), after meeting the required training, sea service and certification criteria
Further opportunities
Senior ETO or shore-based electrical, technical maintenance and fleet-support roles, subject to experience and employer requirements

The Ship Electrician-to-ETO transition is not automatic. DGS has published guidance on pathways from Electro-Technical Rating to ETO, with specified sea-service, training and assessment requirements. Check the current applicable rules before planning this progression.

blocks.text: Strong electrical fundamentals, practical troubleshooting skills, disciplined safety practices and relevant maritime certification can help broaden career options.

For a student aiming to become a Ship Electrician, build a strong foundation in electrical engineering, learn practical troubleshooting and maintenance, and gain supervised experience with electrical equipment.

If the long-term goal is to work as an Electro-Technical Officer aboard merchant ships, choose an eligible electrical or electronics qualification and verify the current approved ETO training, sea-service and certification requirements.

The most important decision is to identify the correct entry route before enrolling: Ship Electrician, Electro-Technical Rating and Electro-Technical Officer are related careers, but they do not necessarily have the same educational requirements, duties or certification pathway.
